patterns.name: Thin Delegator Pattern for Commands
patterns.context: Commands System Overhaul (Enterprise Pipeline #5, Tasks #83-86)
patterns.description: Commands are 3-line markdown shims with `disable-model-invocation: true` that delegate to a single skill. The skill is the source of truth for behavior; the command is the user-facing entry point. Pattern: frontmatter with description and flag, then single line 'Invoke the {skill} skill'.

examples.content:
---
description: Systematic debugging with root cause investigation
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Invoke the debugging skill and follow it exactly as presented to you

---
description: Test-driven development with Red-Green-Refactor
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Invoke the tdd skill and follow it exactly as presented to you

patterns.applicability: All new commands should follow this pattern unless they are standalone utilities (rare exceptions like /setup-pm) or enriched integrations (rare exceptions like /learn)
benefits: Eliminates code duplication - skill logic in one place
Enables skill evolution without command changes
Scalable - 16+ commands follow identical pattern
Clear separation: commands (interface) vs skills (implementation)
exceptions: Enriched commands integrate multiple skills (e.g., /learn uses context-compressor + memory protocol)
patterns.extracted_from: Tasks #83-84, confirmed by QA Task #86

patterns.name: Recursive Descent Parser for Safe Expression Evaluation
patterns.context: Tools System Overhaul Phase C (Task #95) - SEC-TOOL-001 Fix
patterns.description: When code needs to evaluate user-controlled expressions (workflow conditions, config DSLs, template logic), NEVER use new Function(), eval(), or regex-based sanitization. Instead, implement a recursive descent parser that only whitelists safe operations: literals (true/false/numbers/strings), comparisons (===, !==, ==, !=, >=, <=, >, <), logical operators (&&, ||, !), parenthesized grouping. The parser rejects anything it doesn't explicitly support.
patterns.why_it_works: 100% safe because undefined behavior defaults to rejection. Attackers cannot embed code in string literals or bypass pattern matching - parser only recognizes safe token types.
patterns.implementation: SafeExpressionParser class in .claude/lib/workflow/decision-handler.mjs (~200 lines). Tokenizer → Parser → Evaluator. Supports boolean algebra for workflow gate expressions.
patterns.test_coverage: 41 security tests (20 malicious rejections, 16 legitimate expressions, 3 context integration, 2 complex conditions) in tests/lib/workflow/decision-handler-security.test.cjs
patterns.applicability: Any expression evaluation: config files, workflow DSLs, template engines, rule engines, policy languages
anti_patterns: new Function('return ' + userInput)() - arbitrary code execution
eval(sanitized) - bypass via string escaping
Regex blacklist - incomplete, bypassable
patterns.extracted_from: Task #95 (SEC-TOOL-001 fix), validated by 41 passing security tests

patterns.name: Consumer Discovery Pattern for File Relocations
patterns.context: Tools System Overhaul Phase C (Task #95) - 8 library modules relocated from tools/ to lib/
patterns.description: Before relocating ANY file, grep the ENTIRE codebase for: (1) the filename (e.g., 'decision-handler'), (2) the directory path (e.g., 'tools/workflow/'), (3) any require() or import() references to the file. Update ALL consumers before committing. Missing even one import breaks the build, often silently.
patterns.why_critical: Relocated files with missed consumer updates cause MODULE_NOT_FOUND crashes. Example: user-prompt-unified.cjs still referenced old router-state.cjs path after relocation, causing crash on every UserPromptSubmit (Task #47).
update_checklist: Update all require() paths to new location
Update all import paths to new location
Test that all consumers still work
patterns.example: Task #95 relocated 8 modules, updated 45+ consumer imports. Full codebase grep caught all references.
patterns.applicability: Any file relocation, library reorganization, directory restructuring
patterns.extracted_from: Task #95 (8 relocations, 45+ import updates), lessons from Task #47 (missed consumer crash)

patterns.name: Script Phantom Import Regression Testing Pattern
patterns.context: Scripts System Overhaul Pipeline #8 (Tasks #98-99) - identified and prevented phantom imports in package.json and import statements
patterns.description: Create TDD regression tests that validate (1) all package.json scripts reference existing files, and (2) all `import`/`require` statements in script files resolve to valid paths. Two-layer validation catches phantom scripts at both entry points (npm commands) and code level (static imports). Pattern: use regex extraction + filesystem stat() to verify each reference exists.
examples: Phantom package.json scripts: `pnpm validate:agents` referenced non-existent validation tool
Phantom import: `validate-index.mjs` imported from deleted path `.claude/tools/context/context-path-resolver.mjs`
test_structure: Layer 1: Extract all `node <path>` commands from package.json scripts section
Layer 2: Verify each file exists via fs.statSync()
Layer 3: Extract all `import`/`require` statements from script files
Layer 4: Resolve each import to a file and verify it exists
patterns.applicability: Any project with 20+ executable scripts where package.json is the discovery interface
benefits: Prevents broken CI chains (CRITICAL: validate:full was broken at step 5)
Early detection before code review (test runs on every commit)
Self-documenting: test serves as inventory of available scripts
Catches relocations that miss consumer updates
patterns.integration_with_other_patterns: Extends phantom-scripts pattern from Tasks #93-94 (tools); applies to scripts/ directory
patterns.extracted_from: Task #99 (script phantom import fixes), generalizes from Task #93 pattern

patterns.name: TDD Pattern for Security Vulnerability Fixes
patterns.context: Scripts System Overhaul Pipeline #8 (Task #100) - fixed path traversal vulnerability (MEDIUM-001) in install.mjs
patterns.description: When fixing security vulnerabilities, use TDD discipline: (1) write failing test demonstrating the vulnerability exists (RED), (2) implement the fix (GREEN), (3) verify test passes and validates the fix. The test becomes a permanent regression guard against the same vulnerability reappearing. Pattern applies to any class of security defect: path traversal, command injection, expression evaluation, credential exposure.

phases.description: Write test case with malicious input that exploits the vulnerability. Assertion: current code fails or produces unsafe output.
phases.example: path traversal test: `install.mjs --target ../../../etc/passwd` should be rejected, but currently accepts it

phases.description: Implement fix to prevent the vulnerability. Re-run test to verify it now passes.
phases.example: Add validation: reject paths with `..`, check normalized path starts with PROJECT_ROOT

phases.description: Run full test suite to ensure fix doesn't break existing functionality or introduce new vulnerabilities.

vulnerability_details.vulnerability: User could provide target path like `../../../etc` and install to arbitrary locations
vulnerability_details.fix: Two-layer validation: (1) reject `..` literals, (2) check resolved path starts with PROJECT_ROOT
test_cases: Absolute path outside CWD: `/etc/passwd` → REJECTED (unless `--force` flag)
Safe traversal within project: `./src/../target/` → ACCEPTED (resolves to `./target/`)

patterns.applicability: Any security vulnerability (injection, traversal, exposure, overflow, etc.)
benefits: Prevents regression: test permanently guards against this class of vulnerability
Documents the vulnerability for future maintainers
Forces developer to understand the root cause before implementation
Quality gate: test must pass before vulnerability fix is considered done
anti_patterns: Implementing fix without test (impossible to verify fix works)
Test that only checks the happy path (ignores edge cases)
Test that documents the vulnerability but doesn't prevent it
patterns.extracted_from: Task #100 (path traversal fix), proven pattern from TDD literature

patterns.name: Rules Auto-Loading System Prompt Pattern
patterns.context: Rules System Overhaul Pipeline #9 (Task #102-103) - discovered that rules auto-load as system prompt without explicit wiring
patterns.description: In Claude Code, all `.claude/rules/*.md` files are automatically loaded into every conversation's system prompt. Rules do NOT require `require()`, `import`, or explicit references -- they are discovery-based via file globbing. This means: (1) rules are the most reliable enforcement layer for cross-cutting concerns (reach every conversation), (2) every line in a rule costs tokens, so rules must provide 6+ actionable directives to justify cost, (3) thin rules (3-7 lines) are noise not signal, (4) rules are complementary to CLAUDE.md (which spawned agents may not fully absorb).
patterns.why_important: Rules auto-loading is the most reliable way to enforce mandatory agent behaviors like memory protocol and task tracking. Generic CLAUDE.md sections are not guaranteed to be read, but rules in system prompt are always available.

token_cost_analysis.example_thin_rule: 3 lines = ~50 tokens per rule, 9 rules = ~450 tokens baseline
token_cost_analysis.example_expanded_rule: 40 lines = ~350 tokens per rule, 10 rules = ~3500 tokens (7x higher cost)
token_cost_analysis.recommendation: Minimum 6+ directives per rule to justify token overhead. Generic platitudes add noise. Project-specific guidance adds signal.
token_cost_analysis.case_study: Pipeline #9 expanded thin rules from 3-8 lines to 33-54 lines (+250 tokens/rule), but coverage improved (2 new rules filled critical gaps in memory protocol and task tracking)

patterns.applicability: Any project using Claude Code framework with auto-loaded rules
benefits: Rules are guaranteed to reach every conversation (no opt-in required)
Can enforce mandatory agent behaviors without CLAUDE.md bloat
Rule changes propagate automatically (no re-deployment needed)
No wiring complexity (vs agents which need routing, skills which need skill-creator)
patterns.pattern: 1) Identify mandatory cross-cutting behavior (e.g., memory protocol, task tracking). 2) Check if rule exists. 3) If not, create new rule with 6+ directives. 4) If exists and thin (<6 directives), expand with project-specific guidance. 5) Update rule-index.json. 6) Update CLAUDE.md if rule relates to enforcement hooks.
anti_patterns: Creating 3-line rules (generic platitudes without project context)
Duplicating CLAUDE.md content in rules (redundant token use)
Leaving rules out of rule-index.json (breaks programmatic discovery)
Using rules for implementation details that change frequently (use docs instead)
patterns.extracted_from: Task #102-103 (rules audit), validated by learnings.md entries on thin rule expansion

patterns.name: Rule-Index Filesystem Sync Pattern
patterns.context: Rules System Overhaul Pipeline #9 (Task #104) - discovered rule-index.json missing workspace-conventions.md entry
patterns.description: rule-index.json provides programmatic rule discovery (used by rule-selector skill, project-analyzer, and other tools). The index must stay in sync with filesystem. After any rule file operation (create, delete, merge, rename), verify rule-index.json reflects the change. Pattern: file deletion leaves stale index entries; file creation/rename breaks programmatic discovery; merging two files requires removing both old entries and adding merged entry.
sync_checklist: After creating rule: add entry to rule-index.json with description, size, line_count
After deleting rule: remove entry from rule-index.json
After renaming rule: update path and name fields in rule-index.json
After merging rules: remove old entries, add new merged entry
After expanding rule content: update size and line_count fields in rule-index.json
Run `pnpm validate:config` to detect stale entries (validate-rule-index-paths.mjs checks for missing/orphan entries)
patterns.case_study: Pipeline #9 Task #102 found: rule-index.json had 8 entries, but 9 rules existed (workspace-conventions.md was missing). Task #103 created 2 new rules, merged 2 into 1. Task #104 updated rule-index.json to v1.3.0 with 10 rules, 100% coverage.
patterns.applicability: Any project with programmatic rule discovery or auto-loaded rules
benefits: Prevents blind spots in rule discovery (all rules are findable)
Enables programmatic validation (detect missing/orphan rules)
Supports metrics tracking (rule count, coverage, token cost)
Facilitates rule-selector skill (can list all available rules)
prevention: Add pre-commit hook that validates rule-index.json matches filesystem (detect additions/deletions)
Include rule-index.json update in PR checklist for rule changes
patterns.extracted_from: Task #104 (path conflict fixes), rule-index.json v1.3.0 update

patterns.name: Agent Registry Consistency Model
patterns.context: Agents System Deep Dive Pipeline #11 (Task #109) - fixed 3 stale agent name references in rules/agents.md
patterns.description: After any system-wide audit that discovers agent name inconsistencies, fix them in layers: (1) Core registry files (agent-registry.json, agent-config.json) -- source of truth, (2) Routing documentation (rules/agents.md, @AGENT_ROUTING_TABLE.md), (3) Secondary references (catalogs, planning documents). Agent names are widely distributed (49 agents referenced in 46+ places). Fixing layer-by-layer ensures all consumers get updated consistently.
patterns.applicability: Any multi-agent system where agent names can change or agent counts can increase. Useful for: framework audits, agent renames, agent deprecations.
pattern: 1. Audit identifies inconsistency (e.g., rules/agents.md lists old names)
2. Verify source of truth: agent-registry.json is canonical
3. Fix in layers: core registries first, then docs, then secondary references
4. Grep entire .claude/ for old names to find all references
5. Update all references to match agent-registry.json
6. Update rule-index.json if rules are affected
7. Verify no broken imports or references remain
prevention: Add CI validation that agent name references match agent-registry.json
Create pre-commit hook checking for stale agent names
Include agent registry consistency check in post-overhaul checklist

patterns.name: Aggregate Metadata Staleness Detection Pattern
patterns.context: Config System Overhaul Pipeline #10 (Task #106-108) - discovered tool-manifest.json and rule-index-cache.json with stale aggregate counts
patterns.description: Configuration files that contain aggregate counts (e.g., totalAgents, total_rules, totalTools) become stale when their source changes (more agents added, rules merged, tools archived). Unlike rule-index.json (which is indexed per-entry), these aggregates require explicit regeneration. Pattern: identify all files with aggregate counts, create regeneration scripts, add CI validation to detect staleness.

examples.fix: Updated generator to read agent-registry.json instead of hardcoded count
Manually updated after Pipeline #9 rule merges (coding-style + patterns merged into code-standards)

patterns.applicability: Any config system with aggregated counts that derive from dynamic sources
pattern: 1. Identify all config files with aggregate counts
2. Document the source of truth for each aggregate
3. Create automated regeneration script for each aggregate
4. Add CI validation: compare aggregate value against actual source count
5. When source changes (e.g., agents added), regenerate aggregate immediately
prevention: Add `pnpm validate:config-aggregates` script that checks each aggregate against source
Document in config file header: 'This file is auto-generated from X. Run `pnpm regenerate:X` if stale.'
Include aggregate validation in CI pipeline (fail if aggregate != actual count)
When adding/removing items from source, trigger regeneration immediately (not deferred)
patterns.gotcha: Aggregates can become stale quickly if not regenerated immediately after source changes. Pipeline #10 found tool-manifest.json had been stale since agents were increased from 16 to 49 (possibly weeks). This suggests regeneration scripts are not being run automatically.
patterns.extracted_from: Task #106 (audit), Task #107 (fixed phase-models.json), Task #108 (regenerated tool-manifest and rule-index)

patterns.name: Test Archival Must Accompany Implementation Archival
patterns.context: Framework Test Suite Execution (Task #6) validates archival pattern from Task #3
patterns.description: When archiving dead implementation modules, corresponding test files MUST be archived simultaneously to prevent MODULE_NOT_FOUND failures in test runner. Pattern: 1) Identify dead production modules, 2) Grep for all test imports of those modules, 3) Archive test files to test/_archive/ mirroring structure, 4) Verify no orphaned imports remain. This prevents a class of preventable test failures.

examples.scenario: Archive 37 production modules (workflow, memory, ml, self-healing subsystems)
examples.action: Archive corresponding test files: tests/lib/memory/_archive/, tests/lib/workflow/_archive/, tests/phase-4/_archive/, etc.
examples.validation: Grep confirms zero imports of archived modules remain in active test suite

patterns.applicability: Any framework redesign involving dead code removal, especially when test suite is comprehensive and tightly coupled to implementation
benefits: Prevents MODULE_NOT_FOUND crashes in test runner post-archival
Maintains clean separation: active tests for active code, archived tests for archived code
Enables safe refactoring without introducing new test failures
Preserves test history in _archive/ directories for future reference
anti_patterns: Archiving implementation without archiving tests (test failures mislead operators)
Archiving tests but not implementation (orphaned test files create confusion)
Archiving without grep validation (risk of missing indirect imports)
implementation_checklist: 1. Before archival: grep -r 'require.*MODULE_NAME' tests/ to find all imports
2. Create _archive/ directory mirroring test structure
3. Move all test files importing archived modules to _archive/
4. Update git: git mv (which tracks as rename in git status)
5. Verify: grep -r 'archived-module-name' tests/ returns zero matches (excluding _archive/)
6. Run test suite: confirm no new MODULE_NOT_FOUND errors
patterns.extracted_from: Task #3 (dead code archival), Task #4 (system diagnostics), Task #6 (test verification)

patterns.name: Safe Refactoring Validation via Baseline Comparison
patterns.context: Framework archival and consolidation (Tasks #3-5) validated by test suite regression comparison
patterns.description: High-risk refactoring (dead code archival, hook consolidation, test restructuring) should establish baseline diagnostics BEFORE changes, then re-run identical diagnostics AFTER changes to quantify regression risk. Pattern: 1) Run full test suite pre-refactoring, record baseline metrics, 2) Execute refactoring changes, 3) Run identical test suite post-refactoring, 4) Compare results: if pass rate unchanged, zero regression introduced. This provides mathematical certainty that structural changes are safe.

examples.change: Archive 37 dead modules, consolidate 6 hooks into 2, archive 12 test files
examples.verdict: ZERO REGRESSION -- same pass rate, same failures, safe to proceed

patterns.applicability: Any refactoring affecting core infrastructure (hooks, routing, state management, workflow execution)
metrics: Fail count (segmented by pre-existing vs new)
benefits: Mathematical validation of refactoring safety (not just 'feels safe')
Identifies regression immediately if changes break systems
Provides clear evidence for deployment decisions (zero regression → safe to merge)
Enables confident large-scale refactoring without manual testing
anti_patterns: Assuming changes are safe without regression testing
Running different test suite versions (pre vs post) making comparison invalid
Ignoring pre-existing failures (conflating old bugs with new regressions)
validation_checklist: 1. Before refactoring: Run full test suite, record all metrics (pass/fail/skip)
2. Document baseline in diagnostic report with date, commit hash, agent
4. After refactoring: Run IDENTICAL test command, record same metrics
5. Compare: New Failures count should be ZERO (pre-existing failures acceptable)
patterns.extracted_from: Tasks #3-6 (dead code archival + test validation), diagnosed in system-diagnostics-2026-02-08.md

patterns.name: Systematic Integration Pattern with Test-Driven Verification
patterns.context: ADR-100 Cross-Artifact Integration System (Tasks #13-15) - framework-wide integration wiring
patterns.description: When integrating a new system across multiple agents/workflows, follow a systematic approach: (1) Create E2E test first covering all phases, (2) Wire integration points into agents/workflows with health checks, (3) Add self-healing triggers for systemic gaps, (4) Create integration wiring tests to verify all connection points. Each integration point verified by automated tests (not just manual inspection). Pattern: E2E foundation → agent wiring → workflow wiring → validation tests.

phases.description: Create comprehensive end-to-end test that exercises the complete flow. For ADR-100: artifact creation → hook detection → impact analysis → dashboard → bootstrap. Tests all 5 phases of the system.
Wire integration health checks into relevant agents (reflection-agent, evolution-orchestrator). Add skills to frontmatter, add workflow steps, add self-healing triggers.
phases.example: reflection-agent.md Step 4.5 'Integration Health Check', evolution-orchestrator.md Phase E 'Integration Analysis'

phases.description: Update workflows to invoke integration checks at critical phases. Add gate criteria, exit conditions, state schema fields.
phases.example: evolution-workflow.md Phase 6 Actions, Gate Validation Script, Evolution State Schema

phases.description: Create integration wiring tests that verify all connection points: frontmatter skills, workflow sections, Iron Laws, gate criteria, terminology consistency.

patterns.applicability: Any cross-cutting system integration (artifact graphs, error tracking, metrics collection, security auditing, etc.)
benefits: E2E test provides regression safety during wiring
Automated wiring tests prevent integration drift
Systematic approach ensures no integration points missed
Self-healing triggers close feedback loop from detection to remediation
Test-driven verification catches wiring errors immediately
metrics: ADR-100: 65 total tests (44 E2E + 8 reflection + 13 evolution)
Cross-cutting coverage: 5 critical workflows (reflection, evolution, post-creation-validation, artifact-integrator, router)
pattern_components: E2E test covering all phases (creation → analysis → health check → remediation)
Iron Law enforcement (NO ARTIFACT WITHOUT INTEGRATION)
Integration wiring tests (verify all connection points)
Consistent terminology (integration graph, orphaned artifacts, edge count, ADR-100)
anti_patterns: Manual wiring without tests (integration drift inevitable)
Integration as afterthought (add health checks after the fact)
No self-healing triggers (detection without remediation)
Inconsistent terminology (different names for same concept across files)
Partial integration (some agents wired, others missed)
patterns.extracted_from: Tasks #13-15 (ADR-100 integration), validated by 65 passing tests

patterns.name: Framework-Wide Coordination for Cross-Cutting Concerns
patterns.context: ADR-100 Cross-Artifact Integration System - integration health check appears in 4+ workflows/agents
patterns.description: Cross-cutting concerns (integration health, error tracking, metrics, security auditing) require framework-wide coordination to close feedback loops. Pattern: (1) Define core library function (quickIntegrationCheck, trackError, collectMetrics), (2) Wire into multiple agents/workflows at decision points, (3) Add self-healing triggers to detect systemic patterns, (4) Ensure consistent terminology across all integration points. Integration point selection criteria: artifact creation (post-creation-validation), quality assessment (reflection-agent), evolution (evolution-orchestrator), remediation (artifact-integrator).

integration_points: reflection-agent Step 4.5 (quality assessment includes integration health)
evolution-orchestrator Phase E (verify artifact not orphaned)
post-creation-validation Step 11 (trigger reflection for integration assessment)
artifact-integrator skill (analyze gaps and propose tasks)
router Step 0.5 (check integration queue for unprocessed entries)
integration_points.self_healing: Reflection-agent triggers artifact-integrator after detecting 3+ tasks with integration gaps
integration_points.terminology: integration graph, orphaned artifacts, edge count, ADR-100

patterns.applicability: Any cross-cutting concern that needs visibility across multiple agents: error tracking, metrics, security, performance, accessibility, etc.
benefits: Feedback loop closure: detection → assessment → remediation
Framework-wide visibility of cross-cutting metrics
Self-healing triggers prevent systemic issues from accumulating
Consistent terminology enables programmatic processing
coordination_checklist: Define core library function (single source of truth)
Identify integration points (where decisions are made)
Wire into agents/workflows at those decision points
Add self-healing triggers (detect patterns → queue remediation)
Ensure consistent terminology across all integration points
Create integration wiring tests (verify all points connected)
Document the coordination in a reference file (@ENFORCEMENT_HOOKS.md, @WORKFLOW_AGENT_MAP.md)
patterns.example: Integration health coordination: artifact-graph.cjs → 5 integration points (reflection, evolution, post-creation, artifact-integrator, router) → self-healing trigger (3+ gaps → queue) → consistent terminology (graph, orphaned, edge count, ADR-100)
anti_patterns: Single integration point (no cross-cutting visibility)
Inconsistent terminology (each agent uses different names)
No self-healing (detection without remediation)
Manual coordination (no automated tests verify integration points)

patterns.name: Security-First Architecture Pattern for Memory Systems
patterns.context: Memory Management Rebuild (Tasks #7-8, 2026-02-08)
patterns.description: When rebuilding archived modules that handle persistent data (memory, state, config), conduct security review BEFORE implementation planning. Security findings define must-fix mitigations that block implementation. Pattern: Architect designs structure → Security-Architect identifies threats → Planner sequences implementation with security-first steps. This prevents shipping vulnerable code.

examples.sequence: Task #7A (Architect): Design 3-component system → Task #7B (Security-Architect): Identify 3 HIGH risks + must-fix mitigations → Task #8 (Planner): 12-step TDD plan with security utilities first (safeJSONParse, atomicWrites, scrubSensitive)

patterns.applicability: Any system handling persistent data, destructive operations (delete/move/archive), or agent-critical state (memory, config, routing, workflows)
benefits: Prevents shipping vulnerable code (3 HIGH risks caught before implementation)
Security mitigations become blocking prerequisites (MF-001, MF-002, MF-003)
Reduces rework (no post-implementation security fixes)
Test-driven security (22 security test cases: ST-001 through ST-022)
security_findings: T-MEM-001 (HIGH): Archive path injection via date values containing path separators
T-MEM-002 (HIGH): JSON prototype pollution (38 instances of raw JSON.parse across memory subsystem)
I-MEM-001 (HIGH): Sensitive data persists in cold storage (API keys, JWTs, emails) without scrubbing
must_fix_mitigations: MF-001: Create safeJSONParse() utility to strip __proto__, constructor, prototype keys
MF-002: Use atomicWriteSync() for ALL file writes, createBackup() before truncation
MF-003: Implement scrubSensitiveContent() to redact API keys, JWTs, emails before archival
patterns.extracted_from: Tasks #7-8 reflection, Architecture Design + Security Review + Implementation Plan

patterns.name: Integration-First Design Pattern for Module Rebuilds
patterns.context: Memory Management Rebuild (Tasks #7-8, 2026-02-08) - lessons from 900-line archived modules that were never wired
patterns.description: When rebuilding archived modules, start with integration design (how it connects to existing code) before implementation design (what it does internally). The 3 archived memory modules (rotator, pruner, cold-storage) had solid internal designs but zero integration - they were never wired into memory-scheduler.cjs or sync-memory-index.cjs hook. Pattern: Identify trigger points (hook, scheduler, CLI) → Design wiring interfaces → Then design internal logic. Integration coverage is as important as feature completeness.
key_findings: memory-scheduler.cjs has runDeduplication() returning 'disabled (smart-pruner archived)' - ready to wire but not done
memory-scheduler.cjs has runArchiveOldLTM() importing archived cold-storage.cjs - fails silently, zero error visibility
sync-memory-index.cjs hook fires on every memory file write - ideal trigger for rotation, but not wired
issues.md at 53KB is largest memory file, needs immediate rotation, but no module triggers it
archive/learnings-2026-02.md at 463KB is unmanaged warm storage, grows unbounded
patterns.design_principle: Keep each module under 150 lines. Archived modules were 900 lines combined; new design is 300 lines (67% reduction) with better integration coverage.
wiring_checklist: Identify ALL potential trigger points (hooks, schedulers, CLI commands)
Design explicit wiring interfaces (function signatures, error handling, return values)
Document wiring status in component diagram (show trigger → component → storage flow)
Add integration tests verifying wiring (trigger fires → component executes → storage updated)
Create monitoring/logging for silent failures (e.g., 'disabled' stubs should log warnings)
patterns.applicability: Any module restoration from _archive/, especially infrastructure modules (memory, workflow, routing, state management)
benefits: Prevents 'orphan modules' that work internally but are never called
Integration tests catch wiring gaps before deployment
Component diagrams show end-to-end data flow (trigger → logic → storage)
Silent failure monitoring surfaces dead code paths
anti_patterns: Implementing internal logic before designing wiring (the archived modules' mistake)
Assuming scheduler stubs will 'just work' (verify execution path with tests)
Skipping integration tests because 'unit tests pass' (unit ≠ integration)

patterns.name: Multi-Phase Pipeline Validates Wiring Bugs
patterns.context: Phase 4 Code Review (Task #10) + Phase 5 QA Validation (Task #11) of memory management system
patterns.description: When independent code review and QA find the same bugs in different detection methods, it validates those bugs are in the wiring layer (integration interfaces) not in core logic. This pattern applies to any multi-phase review where Unit Tests are insufficient to catch integration issues. Wiring bugs manifest as: (1) Option name mismatches (caller expects X, function parameter is Y), (2) Property name mismatches (returned object has Y, caller accesses X), (3) Type mismatches (caller expects string, function returns number). Keep code review and QA independent (non-redundant) to validate findings with high confidence.

examples.description: memory-scheduler.cjs line 426 accesses pruneResult.entriesRemoved but pruneResolvedEntries() returns { removed: N }
examples.impact: Silent data corruption: undefined + number = NaN in metrics reporting

examples.description: memory-scheduler.cjs line 420 passes { similarityThreshold: 0.6 } but deduplicateFile() accepts { threshold }
examples.impact: Config value silently ignored, function uses default threshold instead of configured value

patterns.why_unit_tests_miss_wiring_bugs: Unit tests validate module functions work correctly in isolation. They don't validate that callers use results correctly. All 41 tests passed, but wiring bugs (C1 & C2) were only caught by code review (static inspection) and QA (integration analysis).
patterns.detection_strategy: Keep code review and QA independent. Code review uses static inspection (does caller match function signature?). QA uses test analysis (does config value reach the function?). Bugs found by both are high-confidence must-fixes.
patterns.applicability: Any system with: configuration-driven modules, interface-dependent components, multiple translation layers (config → code → function), integration wiring across modules
benefits: Wiring bugs detected pre-production (not in customer reports)
Non-redundant reviews: each phase uses different detection method
High confidence: bugs found by multiple phases are real
Fast fixes: wiring bugs typically 1-2 line changes
anti_patterns: Combining code review and QA into single phase (loses redundancy)
Skipping code review because tests pass (misses interface mismatches)
Skipping QA because code review passed (misses integration failures)

patterns.name: Test-Driven Integration Boundary Verification
patterns.context: Tasks #9-13: Memory Management Rebuild discovered 2 integration bugs that 41 unit tests missed
patterns.description: TDD excels at unit-level validation through module isolation, but this isolation can create a blind spot for integration contract mismatches. When Module A tests calls to Module B, the unit test mocks Module B's return values based on test assumptions. If assumptions don't match actual implementation, the mismatch only appears during real integration where mocks are bypassed. Solution: Add explicit 'Integration Verification Phase' after unit tests pass, using REAL modules (not mocks) to verify contracts.
patterns.problem_scenario: Task #9 implemented 4 memory modules with 41 passing unit tests. Task #13 discovered 2 bugs: (1) scheduler assumed pruneResult.entriesRemoved but pruner returns pruneResult.removed, (2) scheduler passed { similarityThreshold: 0.6 } but pruner expects { threshold: 0.6 }. Both bugs found by human code review, not tests.
patterns.root_cause: Unit tests validated internal logic by mocking dependencies based on test assumptions. Integration contract mismatches (field names, parameter names) only visible when code executes together without mocks.

solution_phases.description: Validate internal module logic with mocks/stubs. Example: test that pruner returns { removed: count }
Load REAL modules, call with production parameters, verify contracts match. Example: load actual pruner, verify returned object has 'removed' field, not 'entriesRemoved'
Define explicit contracts for integration points with parameter names, return field names, error cases

patterns.contract_specification_example: const PRUNER_CONTRACT = { deduplicate: { params: { entries: 'array', threshold: 'number' }, returns: { removed: 'number', timestamp: 'string' } } }
patterns.applicability: Any multi-module feature implementation, especially when: parameters have implicit names (not enforced by type system), return values have implicit field names, contract documented in code comments not types, integration has multiple layers
benefits: Catches integration bugs during development (not code review)
Eliminates false confidence: passing tests actually mean integration works
Tests become executable contract specifications
Future refactoring won't break contracts silently
patterns.effort_estimate: Integration tests add 20-30% to TDD cycle (10-15 min per feature for 3-5 integration tests)
prevention_checklist: After writing unit tests, add integration tests using REAL modules
Verify parameter names match actual function signatures
Verify return field names match actual returned objects
Verify error handling is bidirectional (caller + callee)
Document contracts explicitly with expected types/fields
Before declaring feature complete, integration tests must pass
anti_patterns: Only writing unit tests with mocks (creates blind spot for integration)
Assuming contract matches just because unit tests pass
Skipping integration tests because unit tests pass
Documenting contracts in comments but not validating at runtime

patterns.name: Non-Blocking Cross-Cutting Concern Integration
patterns.context: ADR-100 Phase 6 DevOps Integration (Task #12, 2026-02-08)
patterns.description: When integrating operational concerns (artifact integration, error tracking, metrics) into core workflow paths (Router, TaskUpdate), use non-blocking spawning to avoid introducing latency to user requests. The pattern: identify primary path latency budget (e.g., Router <1s), design new concern as spawnable task (not inline), use run_in_background: true, measure overhead (validate <100ms). Example: Router Step 0.5 spawns artifact-integrator with ~20ms overhead, enabling integration analysis without impacting user experience.
key_findings: Router Step 0.5 check adds only ~20ms latency (file read + spawn)
Integration analysis runs in background while user's primary request proceeds
Non-blocking pattern is best for non-critical-path concerns (integration, metrics, profiling, auditing)
Critical path concerns (routing decision, task dispatch) must remain inline
patterns.applicability: Any framework-wide system that must be present but isn't on critical path. Examples: error tracking, metrics collection, profiling, integration analysis, audit logging.
implementation_checklist: 1. Identify primary path latency budget (e.g., Router must respond <1s)
2. Measure current path latency (baseline)
3. Design new concern as spawnable task (not inline processing)
4. Use run_in_background: true or equivalent async wrapper
5. Measure actual latency overhead (validate it's <100ms)
6. Document timeout policy for background tasks
7. Add observability (metrics, logging) for background task completion
benefits: Concerns are always executed (not optional)
No latency impact on user-facing paths
Enables 'good citizenship' — integration runs without impacting UX
Scales to multiple concurrent background tasks via queue
anti_patterns: Adding inline processing to critical path (increases latency)
Making background tasks optional (may be skipped)
No timeout on background tasks (resource accumulation)
Assuming background tasks are sequential (they may interleave)

patterns.name: Intent-Driven Operational Workflow Closure
patterns.context: ADR-100 Phase 6 DevOps Integration (Task #12, 2026-02-08) — routing keywords for artifact-integration intent
patterns.description: When a system (reflection-agent) detects gaps and queues remediation work (integration-queue.jsonl), the Router must have explicit routing keywords to recognize user requests about that concern. Without keywords, user requests would default to developer (incorrect). Task #12 added 11 specific keywords (integrate artifact, orphan artifact, not in catalog, etc.) that route artifact-integration concerns to architect (correct), closing the feedback loop. Pattern: define queue entry types → create routing keywords for each type → map keywords to appropriate agent.
patterns.applicability: Any multi-phase system where earlier phases queue work for later phases. Pattern ensures Router recognizes the queued work when users ask about it.
implementation_checklist: 1. When a system queues work, identify work type (e.g., 'artifact-integration')
2. List natural language phrases users would use (e.g., 'orphan artifact', 'not in catalog')
3. Create routing keywords from those phrases (extract key words, combine variants)
4. Add keywords to routing-table.cjs INTENT_KEYWORDS
5. Map intent to appropriate agent (e.g., artifact-integration → architect)
6. Document in router-decision.md which queues are routed how
7. Add CI check: keywords match queue entry types
benefits: Closes feedback loop: queued work → user request → Router recognition → remediation
Enables operational workflows (users can ask about gaps, get routed to fix)
Prevents default-to-developer anti-pattern (work routed to specialist)
Makes queued work discoverable (not invisible)
anti_patterns: Queuing work without routing keywords (work becomes invisible to Router)
Generic keywords that match many intents (false positives)
Keywords not matching natural language users would use (nobody finds the keywords)
Routing to wrong agent (artifact-integration → developer instead of architect)

patterns.name: Multi-Phase Integration Pipeline with Staged Complexity
patterns.context: ADR-100 Full Implementation (Tasks #1-15, 2026-02-08) — 6-phase systematic integration
patterns.description: Task #12 is the final wiring phase in a 6-phase ADR-100 implementation. The systematic approach (plan → design → core → test → agent-wire → workflow-wire → router-wire → completion) prevents integration gaps. Effectiveness comes from delayed integration — each phase builds on previous phases' concrete artifacts (e.g., artifact-graph.cjs from Task #4 is used by reflection-agent wiring in Task #7). This creates a dependency DAG that naturally orders phases. The 15-task pipeline demonstrates zero missed integration points (5/5 complete), zero design rework, and 100% test pass rate (65/65 tests).
phase_dependency_chain: Task #1-3 (Design): Architect + Security-Architect design, Planner sequences
Task #4-6 (Core+Test): Developer implements artifact-graph, QA tests, test suite validates
Task #7-9 (Agent Wiring): reflection-agent gets Step 4.5, evolution-orchestrator gets Phase E, post-creation gets trigger
Task #10-11 (Workflow Wiring): evolution-workflow gets artifact-integrator call, post-creation-integration hook populates queue
Task #12 (Router Wiring): Router Step 0.5 checks queue, keywords route to architect ← THIS TASK
Task #13-15 (Completion+Learn): artifact-integrator processes queue, diagnostics verify all points, reflection logs learnings
effectiveness_metrics: Execution Time: ~4 hours distributed across 8 sessions
pipeline_health_checklist: All tasks have clear dependencies (no tasks blocking each other)
Each task outputs artifacts that feed into subsequent tasks
Integration points explicitly wired (not assumed to auto-magically work)
Tests verify integration between phases (not just individual components)
No orphaned components (all artifact types assigned to agents)
No rework required (design phase prevents implementation surprises)
Systematic quality gates between phases (no exit without validation)
patterns.applicability: Any enterprise system redesign requiring multi-agent coordination and multi-phase development. Scales to larger pipelines (20+ tasks, 10+ agents).
key_insights: Delayed integration (phase-to-phase dependencies) prevents dangling unintegrated components
Systematic phasing forces consideration of all integration points upfront
Dependency DAG ensures natural ordering without special choreography
Test-driven validation between phases catches gaps before accumulating
anti_patterns: Implementing 'in isolation' without wiring (the archived modules' mistake)
Sequential execution of parallel-able phases (Task #7-9 + Task #10-11 could overlap)
Deferring integration to the end (discovered gaps too late to fix)
No systematic quality gates (rework discovered late in pipeline)
